extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and practitioners in media linguistics and journalism
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying and applying Allan Bell's categories and criteria for what makes events newsworthy and how news language is produced (audience design, textual style, and process-driven values). Useful for analyzing news selection, framing, and linguistic features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negativity
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events with negative aspects (conflict, disaster, crime) are considered more newsworthy; journalists favour negative outcomes when selecting and framing stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recency
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More recent events are prioritized. Timeliness increases newsworthiness and affects whether an event is selected and how it is presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximity
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events closer to the audience (geographically, culturally) are more likely to be selected and emphasized in coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consonance
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that fit existing expectations, stereotypes, or the outlet's narrative framework are easier to report and more likely to be published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unambiguity
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events that can be reported clearly without excessive qualification or complexity are preferred; ambiguity reduces newsability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpectedness
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surprising or novel events attract attention and are more likely to be selected as news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superlativeness
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events characterized by extremes (biggest, worst, first, most) are newsworthy; superlative features are emphasised in copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events judged relevant to the outlet's imagined audience (interests, needs) are prioritized in selection and framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that can be told through individuals or personalities (human-interest angle) are favoured because they engage audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliteness
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Involvement of elites (famous people, politicians, institutions) makes events more newsworthy; prominence of actors is a selection factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events supported by named, credible sources are more publishable; attribution practices affect trust and the story's perceived legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facticity
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of concrete factual details (numbers, places, proper names) increases the story's newsworthiness and readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ongoing stories or those fitting existing coverage beats are continued because they retain audience interest and editorial investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pressure to beat rivals (scoops, exclusives) shapes selection and presentation; competition motivates rapid and sometimes sensational reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-option
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events that can be folded into a current narrative or agenda are useful for editors and are therefore more likely to be covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial need to fill pages or airtime affects which stories are chosen; stories may be selected to balance a bulletin's content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Routine or scheduled events (press conferences, parliamentary sessions) are newsworthy because they are expected and easily covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefabrication
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ready-made stories (press releases, prepared statements) are attractive to newsrooms because they require less reporting effort and slot easily into coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual clarity is a news text value: copy that is easy to understand is preferred for publication and for communicating facts to audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Space/time constraints make brevity a value: concise reporting that fits allocated space is favoured in newswriting and editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vivid, descriptive language (colour) makes stories more engaging and increases their appeal to audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience Design
rubrics_metrics.description: Bell's audience design theory: news language is shaped to address the imagined audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists tailor language, selection, and framing based on who 'our audience' is imagined to be; this affects register, detail, and angles used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverted pyramid
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A structural feature of news text: lead presents most important facts first, followed by decreasingly important details; aids clarity and editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead summarizes key facts
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads (opening sentences/paragraphs) should encapsulate the who/what/when/where/why/how to orient readers quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quote attribution patterns
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patterns for attributing quotes (who said what and how it's presented) are part of news language and shape perceived authority and neutrality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time/place markers
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit temporal and locational markers situate events and increase facticity; they are routine signals in news text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source diversity in citation
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using multiple and varied sources in reporting increases credibility and can affect story selection and framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'shocking', 'surprised', 'first' markers
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lexical markers of surprise, novelty, and primacy are used to make stories appear more newsworthy and engaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension beyond Galtung & Ruge: process and text values
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond Galtung-Ruge: Bell adds process values (continuity, competition, composition, predictability, prefabrication) and text values (clarity, brevity, color).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsworthiness is not only about inherent event characteristics; newsroom processes and textual constraints also determine what becomes news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Storytelling as source of newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition that newsworthiness is partly a property of the storytelling, not just the event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How a story is told — its framing, narrative structure, and linguistic choices — can make an event more or less newsworthy independent of the event's objective features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience-oriented selection
rubrics_metrics.description: News selection follows the logic: what would 'our audience' find newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and journalists make selection choices based on perceived audience interests and values; newsworthiness is therefore audience-relative.
